title: Transitions and Animations
summary: CSS can make a visual change happen over time. A transition moves between values, and an animation can use several steps.
introduction: CSS can make a visual change happen over time. A transition moves between values, and an animation can use several steps. Try a gentle colour change. Learn how to respect people who prefer less movement on a screen.
learningObjectives: Add transitions to state changes and tune duration, timing and delay
Define @keyframes and run them with the animation shorthand
Choose animatable, performant properties and respect prefers-reduced-motion

blocks.text: A transition does nothing on its own. It waits for a property to change, because of `:hover`, `:focus`, a class added by JavaScript, or a media query flipping, and then animates from the old value to the new one instead of jumping. You declare which property to watch (`transition-property`), how long the change takes (`transition-duration`), the speed curve (`transition-timing-function`) and an optional `transition-delay`; the `transition` shorthand takes them in that order and accepts a comma-separated list for several properties. Declare it on the element's normal state so it runs in both directions.

Run it and hover the button: it rises and darkens over 200 milliseconds, then settles back just as smoothly when the pointer leaves. Durations between 150 and 300 milliseconds feel responsive for hover effects; longer ones feel sluggish.

rows: Slow start, fast middle, slow end

blocks.text: Only values with something in between can be animated: lengths, percentages, colours, numbers, transforms and shadows. `display`, `font-family` and `height: auto` have no in-between values, so by default they flip instantly (newer browsers are adding an opt-in, `interpolate-size: allow-keywords`, for animating to `auto`, but it is not yet available everywhere). The classic workaround for an expanding panel is to animate `grid-template-rows` from `0fr` to `1fr`, which does not need to know the final height. Avoid `transition: all`: it animates properties you did not intend and makes the browser check every property on every change.

blocks.title: A transition inside :hover only animates one way
blocks.text: If `transition` is declared in the `button:hover` rule, the change animates when the pointer arrives but snaps back when it leaves: once the hover state ends, the hover rule and its transition no longer apply. Put the `transition` on the element's base rule and only the changed values in `:hover`.

An animation runs by itself as soon as it is applied, and can have as many steps as you like. `@keyframes` names the sequence and lists the values at each point, from `from` to `to` or as percentages. The `animation` shorthand then plays it: name, duration, timing function, delay, iteration count (`infinite` to loop), direction (`alternate` to play backwards every other time) and fill mode (`forwards` to keep the final values when it ends).

blocks.text: Animating `width`, `height`, `top`, `left`, `margin` or `padding` forces the browser to recalculate layout on every frame, which stutters on phones. `transform` (`translate`, `scale`, `rotate`) and `opacity` can be handled by the compositor without touching layout, so they stay smooth even on weak hardware. Move things with `transform: translateX()` rather than `left`, and fade them with `opacity` rather than animating a colour's alpha where you can. `will-change: transform` hints the browser to prepare, but use it sparingly: every hint costs memory.

Some people get dizzy or nauseous from large movements, and every operating system has a "reduce motion" setting that CSS can read. The rule below shortens every animation and transition to practically nothing when that setting is on. Small, functional motion such as a 150ms colour fade is usually fine to keep; parallax, bouncing and sliding content are what the setting is for.

blocks.title: Turn motion off for users who ask for it
Test it
blocks.text: Developer tools can emulate the setting without changing your system: in Chrome and Edge, open the *Rendering* panel and set *Emulate CSS media feature prefers-reduced-motion*; Firefox follows the operating system's setting, or you can set `ui.prefersReducedMotion` to `1` in `about:config`. Toggle it and make sure the page still makes sense without the motion.

questions.question: Which declaration makes a keyframe animation repeat without end?
questions.explanation: `animation-iteration-count: infinite` loops the animation; the shorthand form is the `infinite` keyword inside `animation`.

questions.question: `transition: display 300ms` smoothly fades an element from `display: none` to `display: block`.
questions.explanation: `display` has no in-between values, so it cannot be interpolated. Animate `opacity` or `transform` for the visual effect; newer tools such as `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` only control *when* the `display` switch happens.
